newsitem.title: USA: Judge dismisses class actions against IBM.
newsitem.headline: Judge dismisses class actions against IBM.

text.p: A federal judge has dismissed a group of class action lawsuits against International Business Machines Corp. alleging the company made misleading statements about dividend levels in 1992, according to a written decision made public Wednesday.
The written document followed an oral ruling by U.S. District Judge Jed Rakoff issued from the bench last month granting IBM's motion to throw out the cases.
The lawsuits centred on management comments from Januuary through October 1992 that the company had no plans to reduce its quarterly dividend of $1.21 per share.
The company maintained this position even though it suffered a loss for all of 1991 of $2.8 billion, or $4.95 a share, after charges for restructuring and accounting purposes.
The first three quarters of 1992 brought further bleak news of multi-billion dollar restructuring charges, massive layoffs and downgrading of debt.

After declaration of the fourth quarter dividend on Oct. 27, 1992, IBM comment on the future of its dividend ceased. On Dec. 15, 1992, it said it was unsure of its ability to maintain the dividend at current levels into 1993 and the same day the price of its stock dropped substantially.

The first of a group of class action lawsuits filed by shareholders was filed the next day alleging that IBM's management knew as early as Sept. 30, 1992 that it was unsure it could maintain the dividend level.
Rakoff ruled that the management statements were neither false nor misleading.

He said although the company was "beset by unprecedented economic problems of which the market was made fully aware," IBM's management said its board would continue to declare the company's customary dividend for the immediate future.
"The board responded by doing precisely that," Rakoff said adding that the company continued to fund the dividend into the fourth quarter of 1992 despite anaemic earnings and other problems.

He said that in the face of the continuing decline mangement "prudently" stopped commenting on the dividend and on Dec. 15, 1992 "appropriately" informed the public that it might not be able to maintain the dividend level.
"None of this remotely smacks of fraud," Rakoff wrote.
